knowledgePoints.name: A server with no server
knowledgePoints.teach:
createSdkMcpServer() / create_sdk_mcp_server() builds an MCP server that runs in the same process as your application — no subprocess, no stdio transport, no separate deployment, no serialization boundary between your tool and the rest of your app.

const support = createSdkMcpServer({ name: "support", tools: [lookupOrder] });

This is the SDK's answer to "I need custom tools," and it is the main thing the MCP course does not cover — that course builds external servers over stdio.

Tools from it are referenced as mcp__<server>__<tool> — so the example above gives you mcp__support__lookup_order in allowedTools.

questions.q: Your agent needs three custom tools that call functions already in your app. What do you build?
options: A stdio MCP server as a separate process
An in-process SDK MCP server with createSdkMcpServer
An HTTP MCP server behind your load balancer
Nothing — pass the functions directly in the tools option
questions.explain: The functions are already there. A subprocess would only add a serialisation boundary and a deployment.

questions.q: A server registered as name: "support" holds a tool named "lookup_order". What goes in allowedTools?
questions.explain: Double underscores, mcp prefix. The same naming applies to any MCP server, in-process or not.

reviewQuestions.q: What does an in-process SDK MCP server save you compared with a stdio server?
options: Nothing; it is a convenience alias
A subprocess, a transport, and a separate deployment
The need to write tool descriptions
reviewQuestions.explain: Same protocol, no process boundary. The naming prefix stays.

knowledgePoints.name: Function in TypeScript, decorator in Python
knowledgePoints.teach:
tool() has a different shape in each language, and the docs are easy to skim past:

TypeScriptPython
FormA function returning a definitionA decorator on an async function
Signaturetool(name, description, inputSchema, handler, extras?)@tool(name, description, input_schema, annotations?)
SchemaZod (3 or 4)Type map {"a": float} or full JSON Schema
HandlerThe 4th argumentThe decorated function itself
AnnotationsInside extras.annotationsThe 4th positional argument

Both return {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": ...}]} from the handler.

questions.q: In Python, where does the handler live in a @tool definition?
options: It is the decorated async function itself
questions.explain: Decorator form: the function you decorate is the handler. TypeScript passes it as the 4th argument instead.

questions.q: Where do annotations go in each language?
options: extras.annotations in TypeScript; fourth positional argument in Python
questions.explain: The 4th slot is the handler in TypeScript and annotations in Python — which is exactly why this is worth drilling.

knowledgePoints.name: The TypeScript-only extras
knowledgePoints.teach:
TypeScript's extras carries two things Python has no equivalent for:

  • searchHint — a one-line capability phrase shown in the deferred-tool list when tool search is active. It is how a tool advertises itself before its full schema is loaded.
  • alwaysLoad: true — keep this tool's full schema in the initial prompt instead of deferring it. For the two or three tools an agent needs constantly.

Both exist because a large tool surface is expensive to describe up front, so schemas get deferred until needed.

questions.q: What is searchHint for?
options: A one-line capability phrase shown in the deferred-tool list before the full schema loads
Ranking results returned by the tool
questions.explain: It is how a deferred tool makes itself findable without paying for its whole schema.

questions.q: A tool is needed on nearly every turn and you do not want its schema deferred. Which extra?
questions.explain: alwaysLoad keeps it in the initial prompt. Use it sparingly — that is context you are spending every turn.

reviewQuestions.q: What do handlers return, in both languages?
reviewQuestions.explain: The MCP content-block shape. isError sits alongside it on the result, not in place of it.

knowledgePoints.name: Hints, and their surprising defaults
knowledgePoints.teach:
ToolAnnotations are behavioural hints, not security controls. Clients should not rely on them for security decisions.

  • title
  • readOnlyHint — default false
  • destructiveHint — default true
  • idempotentHint — default false
  • openWorldHint — default true

The defaults are deliberately pessimistic: an undeclared tool is assumed to be destructive and to touch the outside world. Two of the five default to true, and both of those are the cautious answer.

questions.q: Is readOnlyHint: true enough to guarantee a tool cannot modify anything?
options: No — annotations are hints and must not be relied on for security
Yes, but only for MCP tools
questions.explain: Real restriction comes from tool sets, disallowedTools, and hooks. The hint just tells the model what to expect.

questions.q: Which two ToolAnnotations default to true?
questions.explain: Pessimistic defaults: assume it breaks things and assume it reaches the outside world until told otherwise.

reviewQuestions.q: Where does real tool restriction come from, if not annotations?
reviewQuestions.explain: Withhold it, block it, or gate it. Those are the three that actually hold.

knowledgePoints.name: Four shapes, and reproducibility
knowledgePoints.teach:
• mcpServers — a record of configs, in four shapes: stdio, SSE, HTTP, and the in-process SDK server.
  • strictMcpConfig: true — use only the servers passed in mcpServers, ignoring project .mcp.json, user settings, plugin servers, and claude.ai connectors. Reach for this when you need a reproducible tool surface in production.
  • toolAliases — map a built-in tool name onto an MCP tool so Claude calls yours instead, e.g. { Bash: 'mcp__workspace__bash' }.
  • AgentDefinition.mcpServers — servers scoped to a single subagent.

questions.q: Your staging agent keeps picking up a developer's personal MCP server. Which option stops that?
questions.explain: settingSources governs settings files; strictMcpConfig is the one that shuts out .mcp.json, plugin servers, and connectors as well.

questions.q: What does toolAliases let you do?
options: Rename your MCP tools for readability
Map a built-in tool name onto an MCP tool so Claude calls yours instead
Alias one MCP server to another
questions.explain: e.g. { Bash: 'mcp__workspace__bash' } — the model reaches for Bash and gets your sandboxed implementation.

reviewQuestions.q: Name the four mcpServers config shapes.
reviewQuestions.explain: The fourth one — in-process — is the one that only exists inside the SDK.

knowledgePoints.name: The description is the selection mechanism
knowledgePoints.teach:
The tool description is the primary mechanism the model uses to select a tool.

So when an agent confuses two similar tools, the highest-leverage fix is expanding each description — input formats, example queries, edge cases, and explicit boundary statements about when not to use it. Not few-shot examples in the system prompt. Not merging the two tools into one.

A description doing its job:

"Look up an order by ID. Accepts a 12-character alphanumeric order ID
 (e.g. NS4417XQ2210). Returns status, line items, and refund eligibility.
 Use get_customer first if you only have an email address."

Note the last sentence. Half of good description design is telling the model what the other tool is for.

questions.q: An agent keeps calling search_orders when it should call search_customers. Highest-leverage fix?
options: Add few-shot examples to the system prompt
Expand both descriptions with input formats, example queries, edge cases, and boundaries
Merge the two tools into one
questions.explain: Glossary t14, and exam sample question 2. Selection is driven by the description, so that is where the fix belongs.

questions.q: What makes "Use get_customer first if you only have an email address" a good line in a description?
options: It documents the API for developers
It tells the model when NOT to use this tool, which is half of selection
questions.explain: Boundaries disambiguate. A description that only says what a tool does still competes with its neighbours.

reviewQuestions.q: Which four things belong in a description that has to disambiguate against a similar tool?
options: Input formats, example queries, edge cases, and boundary explanations
Rate limits, latency, cost, and region
A JSON schema and nothing else
reviewQuestions.explain: The schema says what is accepted; the description says when to reach for it.

knowledgePoints.name: The one field that is actually in the protocol
knowledgePoints.teach:
isError is a real MCP field. It is how a tool result signals failure back to the calling agent.

The alternative — returning a success payload whose text happens to say "could not find that order" — is worse than it looks. The agent has to infer failure from prose, which it will sometimes do wrong, and any code you write around the result cannot branch on it at all.

Exam glossary t15. When the question asks which of the three named error fields belongs to the protocol, this is the one.

questions.q: Which of isError, errorCategory and isRetryable is defined by MCP?
questions.explain: One real field, two conventions. The exam names all three, which is exactly why the distinction is tested.

questions.q: Why is returning failure as ordinary success text a problem?
options: The agent must infer failure from prose, and your code cannot branch on it
questions.explain: Both consumers lose. Signalling is cheap; inference is not reliable.

options: Telling the SDK to retry the call
Signalling failure on a tool result back to the calling agent
reviewQuestions.explain: Signalling, not retrying. Whether to retry is your own isRetryable convention.

knowledgePoints.name: errorCategory and isRetryable are yours
knowledgePoints.teach:
Read this carefully, because the exam names three things and only one is a protocol field.

  • errorCategory — not an SDK or MCP field. It is a design convention: you classify failures in your own error payload (transient / validation / business / permission) so the agent can pick the right recovery instead of guessing from prose. (Glossary t16.)
  • isRetryable — likewise your own field, a boolean saying whether the operation can safely be retried. isRetryable: false on a business error means don't retry — explain the business-rule violation instead. (t17.)

Learn them as vocabulary; just don't go looking for them in the SDK types.

questions.q: A refund is denied by policy. What should isRetryable be, and what should the agent do?
options: true — retry with a smaller amount
false — explain the business-rule violation instead of retrying
true — the policy engine may be flaky
Leave it unset; the SDK infers it
questions.explain: A business rule will not change on the second attempt. Retrying just burns turns and looks broken to the customer.

questions.q: Where would you find errorCategory in the SDK type definitions?
options: Nowhere — it is a convention you implement in your own payload
questions.explain: Exam vocabulary, author-defined field. Knowing that it is a convention is itself the tested fact.

knowledgePoints.name: The four categories, used
knowledgePoints.teach:
The point of a category is that each one implies a different recovery:

  • transient — retry, probably with backoff.
  • validation — fix the arguments and call again.
  • business — do not retry; explain the rule to the user.
  • permission — do not retry; escalate or ask for authorisation.

Without the category, all four look the same to the model: a string that says something went wrong. With it, the agent's next move is determined rather than guessed.

questions.q: Which category implies "fix the arguments and call again"?
questions.explain: The call was malformed, not forbidden. That is a different recovery from either retry or escalate.

questions.q: What is the actual argument for categorising errors at all?
options: Each category implies a different recovery, so the agent's next move stops being a guess
questions.explain: Undifferentiated failure text gives the model one behaviour for four situations.

reviewQuestions.q: Which of these three is a real MCP field: isError, errorCategory, isRetryable?
reviewQuestions.explain: Drill this one — the exam treats all three as named concepts, which makes the distinction easy to lose.

knowledgePoints.name: What a coordinator can actually recover from
knowledgePoints.teach:
A subagent times out halfway through. Four things it could hand back:

  1. An empty result marked successful. Worst. The coordinator now believes a sub-topic was covered and was found to contain nothing.
  2. A generic "unavailable" string after silent retries. The coordinator learns that something failed, and nothing else.
  3. Nothing at all. The coordinator hangs or times out itself.
  4. A structured error naming what failed and how far it got. Best.

A coordinator can only make an intelligent recovery decision from information it actually receives.

And recall why this is sharp with subagents specifically: only the final message crosses back. Whatever partial progress the subagent made is invisible unless the final message says so.

questions.q: A subagent times out halfway. What should the coordinator receive?
options: An empty result marked successful, so the run continues
A structured error naming what failed and how far it got
A generic "unavailable" string after silent retries
Nothing, so the coordinator can time out and retry
questions.explain: Partial progress plus a named failure is the only payload that supports an intelligent next move.

questions.q: Why is 'empty result marked successful' the most dangerous of the four?
options: It converts a failure into a false finding the coordinator will act on
It causes the SDK to retry indefinitely
questions.explain: Silence reported as a finding is worse than an error, because nothing downstream will question it.

reviewQuestions.q: Why do silent retries inside a subagent hurt the coordinator?
options: They hide both the failure and the partial progress, leaving the coordinator with nothing to act on
reviewQuestions.explain: Retrying is fine; retrying invisibly is what destroys the information the coordinator needed.
